6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
cContains sulfur atom in their side chain
  • Cysteine
    • Polar
    • Uncharged
    • Contain thiol group (-CH2SH) which can form disulfide bonds
  • Methionine
    • Non-polar
    • Contain thioether group (–CH₂SCH₃)
    • Plays critical role in protein synthesis and methylation
Both contain sulfur. How do cysteine and methionine differ?
Cysteine: polar, uncharged, has a thiol that can form disulfide bonds.
Methionine: non-polar, has a thioether, and is key in protein synthesis and methylation.
6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
dContains carboxyl (-COOH or -COO-) in the side chain
  • Polar
  • Hydrophilic
  • Negatively charged
  • Ionise (-COOH to -COO-) at physiological pH (pH 7.4)
  • Glutamic acid or glutamate and aspartic acid or aspartate
Which amino acids are negatively charged at physiological pH (7.4)?
Glutamate and aspartate. Their side chain -COOH ionises to -COO-.
6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
eContains amide group (-CONH2) in the side chain
  • Polar
  • Hydrophilic
  • Uncharged
  • Do not ionize
  • Glutamine and Asparagine
Glutamine and asparagine are polar. Are they charged?
No. Their amide group (-CONH2) is uncharged and does not ionize.
6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
fContains basic side chain
  • Polar
  • Positively charged
  • Hydrophilic
  • Lysine (pKa = 10.5) and Arginine (pKa = 12.5) - Protonated at physiological pH
  • Histidine (pKa = 6) – mostly deprotonated at physiological pH but side chain can easily release and accept proton even with a minimal change in pH

Mnemonic: Basic Healthy Lifestyle Advice

Basic – Histidine Lysine Arginine

Lysine and arginine are protonated at physiological pH. What about histidine?
Mostly deprotonated (pKa = 6), but its side chain easily releases and accepts a proton with a minimal change in pH.
6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
gContains aromatic side chain
  • Tryptophan and phenylalanine: Hydrophobic and non-polar because of the aromatic ring
  • Tyrosine: Hydrophilic and polar because the aromatic ring is attached to -OH group
All three are aromatic. Why is tyrosine polar while phenylalanine and tryptophan are non-polar?
Tyrosine's aromatic ring is attached to an -OH group, making it hydrophilic and polar.
6 · Classification of standard amino acids
1. Classification by chemical structure – depending on the variation in the R-chain
hContain aliphatic cyclic side chain
  • Non-polar
  • Hydrophobic
  • Proline (P; Pro)
Which amino acid has an aliphatic cyclic side chain?
Proline (P; Pro), which is non-polar and hydrophobic.

Classification by polarity & metabolic fate

2) Classification by polarity

- All hydrophilic amino acids are polar

- All hydrophobic amino acids are non-polar

7 · Classification of standard amino acids

Quick check: metabolic & nutritional

Which amino acids are purely ketogenic?
Leucine and Lysine.
Which amino acids are both glucogenic and ketogenic?
Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, Tyrosine, Isoleucine.
What is the difference between a ketogenic and a glucogenic amino acid?
Ketogenic: breaks down into acetyl-CoA or acetoacetyl-CoA, which can be converted into ketone bodies.
Glucogenic: breaks down into precursors for glucose synthesis during gluconeogenesis.
Expand the mnemonic PVT TIM HALL.
Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, Histidine, Arginine, Lysine, Leucine.
Why is arginine called conditionally essential?
It can be derived from ornithine in the urea cycle in amounts sufficient for adults, but more may be needed from the diet during rapid growth or severe illness.
7 · Classification of standard amino acids

Example of question: FROM NOTES

A 22-year-old patient develops severe intestinal malabsorption. Despite receiving adequate energy, the patient develops a negative nitrogen balance because an amino acid required for protein synthesis is poorly absorbed. Which of the following amino acids is most likely deficient in this patient?

  • A. Alanine
  • B. Aspartate
  • C. Tyrosine
  • D. Threonine
Answer: D. Threonine. Threonine is an essential amino acid (PVT TIM HALL), so the body cannot make it and it must be absorbed from the diet. Alanine, aspartate and tyrosine are non-essential and can be synthesized by the body.

8 · Level of organisation

Level of Organisation

8 · Level of organisation

Primary structure

Primary

Amino acids linked together by peptide bond

Does all protein has primary structure?
Yes. Every protein is built from one or more chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, so every protein has a primary structure (its amino acid sequence).
8 · Level of organisation

Secondary structure

Two most common secondary structure are alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet.

Alpha-helix

  • Usually right handed
  • Each turn in the helix consume about 3.6 amino acid residues and has the diameter of 1.5 A.
  • Stabilised by hydrogen bond in between NH and C=O
8 · Level of organisation

Secondary structure

Beta-pleated sheet

  • side-by-side arrangement of extended beta strand
  • Stabilised by hydrogen bond in between NH and C=O
Does all primary structure has to proceed to fold into secondary structure?
No. Some regions stay as loops or random coil, and some proteins or segments (intrinsically disordered regions, short peptides) never form a stable α-helix or β-sheet.
8 · Level of organisation

Tertiary structure

Denotes the 3-dimensional structure of the whole protein.

Stabilized by several bonds: hydrogen bond, hydrophobic bonds, electrostatic bonds, van der Waals forces and disulfide bridge.

Can a protein form tertiary structure without having secondary structure?
Metallothionein (cysteine rich proteins)
Yes. Metallothionein has almost no α-helix or β-sheet. Its 3-D fold is held together by metal ions bound to its cysteine side chains.
8 · Level of organisation

Quaternary structure

More than one polypeptide chain termed as subunit or monomer, fold together to form one whole protein

Stabilized by several bonds: hydrogen bond, hydrophobic bonds, electrostatic bonds, van der Waals forces and disulfide bridge.

Can a protein from secondary structure directly fold into quaternary structure?
Collagen
Yes. In collagen, three helical chains (secondary structure) wind directly around each other into a triple helix, without a separate globular tertiary fold.
What is the difference between the hydrogen bond formed in secondary structure and the hydrogen bond formed in tertiary and quaternary structure?
Secondary: between backbone atoms (NH and C=O of peptide bonds).
Tertiary / quaternary: mainly between side chains (R-groups), within one chain (tertiary) or between different subunits (quaternary).
8 · Level of organisation

Quick check: levels of organisation

What stabilises both the alpha-helix and the beta-pleated sheet?
Hydrogen bonds between NH and C=O.
How many residues are in each turn of an alpha-helix, and which way does it usually turn?
About 3.6 residues per turn. The helix is usually right handed.
What makes a structure quaternary?
More than one polypeptide chain (subunits/monomers) fold together to form one whole protein, e.g. haemoglobin.
9 · Bonds in protein structure

Covalent bonds:

  • Peptide bond
  • Disulfide bridge →

Disulfide bridge

Which amino acid: Cysteine

How it is formed: oxidation of 2 cysteine sidechains

How to break a disulfide bond: chemical reduction using reducing agent (e.g: Glutathione), that donates electron or hydrogen atom to split the sulfur-sulfur link

9 · Bonds in protein structure

Non-covalent bonds:

Hydrogen bond

  • Definition: A bond formed when a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to an electronegative atom (e.g., O, N, or F) interacts with another electronegative atom nearby.
  • Which amino acid can form hydrogen bond: all

Hydrophobic interaction

  • Occurs only between amino acid side chain
  • Which amino acid: non-polar hydrophobic amino acids
  • Function: they usually form the core of a protein, aid it protein dimerizarion

Van der Waals interaction

  • Weak interaction and short range
  • Arises from fluctuation of electrons density that creates a temporary dipole moment
  • Which amino acid: All 20 amino acids - can form weak temporary dipoles when packed close to nearby atoms
  • Facilitate tight packing of atoms in protein especially in hydrophobic core in tertiary and quaternary structure
9 · Bonds in protein structure

Non-covalent bonds:

Ionic bond

  • Definition: Negatively charged group on one amino acid side chain interact with positively charged groups on another amino acid side chain
  • Which amino acid: Polar and charged (lysine, arginine, histidine, glutamate and aspartate)

Electrostatic interaction

  • Ionic bonds are a specific type of electrostatic interaction.
  • Other examples of electrostatic interactions are
    • dipole-dipole interaction (interaction between two polar amino acid side chains with partial positive and partial negative charges)
    • charge-dipole interaction (interaction between fully charged amino acid side chain and partially charged amino acid side chain)
9 · Bonds in protein structure

Quick check: bonds

Name the two covalent bonds in protein structure.
Peptide bond and disulfide bridge.
How is a disulfide bridge formed, and how is it broken?
Formed: oxidation of 2 cysteine side chains.
Broken: chemical reduction with a reducing agent (e.g. glutathione).
Which amino acids can form hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions?
All amino acids can form both.
Which interaction usually forms the core of a protein?
Hydrophobic interaction between non-polar side chains, with van der Waals forces packing the core tightly.
Which amino acids can form ionic bonds?
Polar, charged ones: lysine, arginine, histidine, glutamate and aspartate.
Dipole-dipole vs charge-dipole interaction: what is the difference?
Dipole-dipole: two polar side chains with partial charges.
Charge-dipole: a fully charged side chain with a partially charged one.

10 · Protein structure – function relationship

Quick check: structure – function

How does protein folding allow an enzyme to work?
Folding creates an active site where only a specific substrate binds, and the reaction is catalysed.
What gives collagen its tensile strength?
Its triple-helix structure. Tropocollagen consists of three fibres (each about 1000 amino acids) bundled together in the collagen triple helix.
What is cooperative binding in haemoglobin?
When O2 binds to deoxyhemoglobin, it causes a conformational change that makes the other 3 heme groups more likely to bind O2. This allosteric property results from the quaternary structure.
What stabilises insulin's tertiary structure so it binds its receptor precisely?
Disulfide bonds: two interchain and one intrachain.
10 · Protein structure – function relationship

Quick check: misfolding & mutations

Name two amyloidogenic proteins and their diseases.
Amyloid-β (Aβ), cleaved from APP, forms amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's disease.
Prion protein (PrP) misfolds into the scrapie form (PrPSc) and causes neurodegenerative disease through protein templating.
What is the mutation in sickle cell anaemia (HbS)?
At the 6th amino acid of the β chain, glutamic acid (hydrophilic) is replaced by valine (hydrophobic). HbS then polymerises when deoxygenated, which distorts red blood cells into a sickle shape.
Hb Hikari, Hb S and Hb M (Boston): which amino acid change causes each?
Hb Hikari: β chain, 61 Lysine → Asparagine
Hb S: β chain, 6 Glutamate → Valine
Hb M (Boston): α chain, 58 Histidine → Tyrosine
What is a haemoglobinopathy? Give the most common examples.
A condition in which a mutation in the Hb genes compromises biological function. The most common are the thalassemias (alpha- and beta-) and sickle cell disease (SCD).
